name: Ginger
aka: Sheng Jiang, Gan Jiang, Zingiber officinale
summary: Cochrane reviews and meta-analyses confirm ginger works for pregnancy, chemotherapy and postoperative nausea at about 1-1.5 g daily. Gingerols inhibit COX-2 and 5-LOX, modestly easing osteoarthritis pain, and a 2018 meta-analysis showed lower fasting glucose and HbA1c.
how: Fresh tea: steep 1-2 inches of sliced root in 8 oz boiling water 10-15 minutes, 2-3 cups daily. Dried powder 250 mg-1 g capsules 2-4 times daily; for nausea, 250 mg every 6 hours or chew crystallized ginger. Use liberally in cooking.
safety: May increase bleeding risk, so use cautiously with warfarin, aspirin and clopidogrel and stop 1-2 weeks before surgery. Doses above 5 g/day cause heartburn, diarrhea and mouth irritation. May lower blood sugar alongside diabetes medication. Generally safe in pregnancy under 1 g/day, but check with your OB/GYN.
origin: A foundational TCM herb: fresh ginger warms the Lungs and expels cold, dried ginger warms the Spleen and Stomach.

name: Ginseng
aka: Ren Shen, Xi Yang Shen, Panax ginseng
summary: A 2020 meta-analysis of 10 RCTs found improved cognition, especially reaction time and working memory, and a 16-RCT review found significantly lower fasting glucose. Red Korean ginseng shows moderate benefit for erectile dysfunction, and it reduces cancer-related fatigue.
how: Standardized extract 200-400 mg daily (4-7% ginsenosides). Decoction: simmer 3-6 root slices 30-60 minutes, once or twice daily. Tincture 1-2 mL two to three times daily. TCM advises cycling: 2-3 weeks on, then 1-2 weeks off, to avoid overstimulation.
safety: Can cause insomnia, headache, digestive upset and agitation, especially Asian ginseng. May interact with warfarin, diabetes medications (hypoglycemia), MAOIs and stimulants. Avoid in uncontrolled hypertension and in estrogen-sensitive conditions (mild estrogenic activity). Not recommended during acute febrile infection.
origin: The 'King of Herbs', tonifying Qi and calming the spirit; American ginseng is used when heat signs are present.

name: Astragalus
summary: Polysaccharides and astragalosides stimulate macrophages, NK cells and T-lymphocytes. A 2019 meta-analysis of 62 RCTs found astragalus injection plus conventional care improved ejection fraction and BNP in heart failure; a 2016 Cochrane review found formulas may aid chemotherapy as complementary support.
how: Add 9-15 g dried root slices to soups or simmer 30+ minutes as a decoction, then remove the fibrous root. Powder or capsules 500-1000 mg standardized extract 2-3 times daily; tincture 2-4 mL three times daily. Classic food therapy simmers it with chicken, goji berries and jujube dates.
safety: Very well tolerated. Avoid during acute febrile infection, as tonics are not used during active illness in TCM. May interact with immunosuppressive drugs (transplant and autoimmune medications) by stimulating immunity, and theoretically with lithium via diuretic effect. Use only verified A. membranaceus, since other Astragalus species contain toxic swainsonine.
origin: A premier Qi tonic that strengthens Wei Qi, the defensive energy, and promotes healing of chronic sores.

name: Reishi Mushroom
summary: Beta-glucans and ganoderic acids modulate immunity. A 2016 Cochrane review found reishi stimulated host immunity and patients were 1.27x more likely to respond to chemo or radiotherapy as complementary support alongside standard care, never replacing it; 1.8 g extract also reduced fatigue in neurasthenia.
how: Extract capsules 1.5-9 g dried extract daily, or 1-1.5 g concentrated extract specifying beta-glucan and triterpene content. Decoction: simmer 5-10 g sliced dried reishi 2+ hours (very bitter). Dual-extraction tinctures capture both compound classes; powder mixes into coffee.
safety: May increase bleeding risk and interact with anticoagulants and immunosuppressants; stop 2 weeks before surgery. Can lower blood pressure, so use caution on antihypertensives. Side effects include dry mouth, dizziness, nosebleeds and digestive upset, and rare hepatotoxicity has been reported with powdered products, so use reputable sources.
origin: The 'Mushroom of Immortality', reserved for emperors; nourishes the Heart and calms the Shen.

name: Lion's Mane Mushroom
summary: Hericenones and erinacines stimulate nerve growth factor synthesis. A 2009 double-blind RCT found 3 g/day for 16 weeks significantly improved cognitive scores in adults with mild cognitive impairment (benefits faded after stopping), and a 2010 RCT reduced depression and anxiety scores.
how: Standardized extract 500-1000 mg two to three times daily, ideally standardized to hericenones and erinacines. Powder 3-5 g dried mushroom daily in coffee, smoothies or soup; fresh mushroom can be seared like a steak. Cognitive benefits require consistent use over weeks to months.
safety: Generally very safe with few reported side effects. Possible allergic reactions in those sensitive to mushrooms, and mild initial digestive discomfort. May slow blood clotting, so use caution before surgery. There is a theoretical concern about stimulating NGF in certain cancers, though no evidence of this in practice.
origin: Used in TCM to strengthen the Spleen, nourish the Stomach and calm the mind; prized as the 'monkey head mushroom'.

name: Cordyceps
aka: Dong Chong Xia Cao, Cordyceps militaris/sinensis
summary: A 2017 RCT found Cordyceps militaris improved VO2max by 7% after 3 weeks, with cordycepin increasing ATP production. A systematic review of 22 Chinese RCTs found it improved serum creatinine as an adjunct in chronic kidney disease.
how: Cultivated C. militaris extract 1-3 g daily, the affordable and sustainable option with equal or greater cordycepin than wild cordyceps. CS-4 fermented mycelium 1.5-3 g daily is the form used in most clinical studies. Powder blends into smoothies, coffee or broth, or simmer with chicken as a tonifying soup.
safety: Generally well tolerated, with mild GI upset, dry mouth or nausea possible. Theoretical interaction with immunosuppressive drugs and caution with anticoagulants, since it may slow clotting. May lower blood sugar, so monitor if diabetic on medication. Avoid if allergic to molds or fungi, and use cautiously with hormone-sensitive conditions.
origin: 'Winter worm, summer grass', a prized tonic for both Kidney Yang and Lung Yin, used for breathlessness and fatigue.

name: Turmeric / Curcumin
summary: Curcumin inhibits NF-kB, COX-2 and inflammatory cytokines. A 2016 meta-analysis of 8 RCTs found significantly reduced osteoarthritis pain comparable to ibuprofen, a 2017 meta-analysis found antidepressant-scale benefit, and trials support it as complementary support in colorectal, pancreatic and breast cancer.
how: Standardized curcumin extract 500-1000 mg daily with black pepper (piperine) and a fat source, since absorption alone is under 1%. Phytosome forms such as Meriva 500-1000 mg daily absorb far better. Golden milk: 1 tsp turmeric plus a pinch of pepper in warm milk with honey; cook with turmeric plus oil and pepper.
safety: High-dose supplements cause GI upset, nausea and diarrhea. Curcumin inhibits platelet aggregation, so use caution with anticoagulants, and it may lower blood sugar. Avoid concentrated supplements with gallstones or bile duct obstruction. High doses raise oxalate (kidney stone risk) and may interact with certain chemotherapy drugs, so consult your oncologist. Food amounts are safe for nearly everyone.
origin: In TCM Jiang Huang invigorates Blood and moves Qi, used for pain from Blood stasis in the shoulders and arms.

name: Green Tea
aka: Lu Cha, Camellia sinensis, matcha, EGCG
summary: A 2020 study of over 100,000 Chinese adults found habitual tea drinkers had 20% lower heart disease and stroke risk and lived 1.26 years longer. A 17-RCT meta-analysis found reduced fasting glucose and HbA1c; EGCG intake is associated with modestly lower risk of several cancers.
how: Brew at 160-180 F (not boiling) for 2-3 minutes, re-steeping leaves 2-3 times. Aim for 3-5 cups daily, the intake linked to benefit. Matcha delivers the whole leaf. EGCG supplements 300-500 mg daily, though whole tea is generally preferred for synergy.
safety: Contains 30-50 mg caffeine per cup, causing insomnia, anxiety or jitteriness in sensitive people. EGCG supplements above 800 mg/day have been linked to liver toxicity, so keep supplement doses moderate or drink tea instead. Tannins reduce iron absorption, so avoid with iron-rich meals if anemic. May interact with beta-blockers such as nadolol, blood thinners and stimulants, and can reduce absorption of some medications.
origin: In TCM green tea clears heat, resolves toxins and calms the mind; tea's discovery is credited to emperor Shennong.

name: Goji Berries
aka: Gou Qi Zi, wolfberry, Lycium barbarum
summary: Among the richest dietary sources of zeaxanthin: a 2011 RCT found 15 g/day for 90 days raised plasma zeaxanthin 26% and protected against macular hypopigmentation, an early sign of macular degeneration. A 2009 RCT showed enhanced immune response to influenza vaccine in elderly subjects.
how: Eat 15-30 g dried berries daily as a snack or in oatmeal, trail mix and salads. Tea: steep a handful in hot water 10 minutes and eat the berries afterward. Add to chicken soup with astragalus and jujube dates, or blend into smoothies.
safety: May interact with warfarin via CYP2C9, with several case reports of raised INR. Can lower blood sugar, so monitor on diabetes medications, and may add to blood pressure medications. Possible allergic reactions in people allergic to nightshades such as tomatoes and peppers. Safe in food amounts.
origin: A premier Yin tonic that nourishes Liver and Kidney and 'brightens the eyes'; a staple of TCM tonic soups.

name: Schisandra
aka: Wu Wei Zi, five-flavor berry, Schisandra chinensis
summary: An adaptogen studied extensively by Soviet researchers; schisandrin B modulates cortisol and the HPA axis and is potently hepatoprotective, with the derivative DDB approved as a liver drug in several Asian countries. A 2017 review found improved attention and processing speed under stress.
how: Chew 1-3 g dried berries daily, or steep 5-10 berries in hot water 10 minutes as tea. Tincture 1-2 mL two to three times daily; standardized extract 500-1000 mg daily. Traditionally brewed with goji berries and chrysanthemum as a balancing tonic tea.
safety: Can stimulate uterine contractions, so avoid in pregnancy. May interact with drugs metabolized by CYP3A4 and CYP1A2 and with CNS-active medications, and may lower the seizure threshold, so use caution with epilepsy medications. May cause heartburn and reduced appetite; not recommended during acute febrile infection.
origin: Named for containing all five tastes, so it enters all five Yin organs, astringing Lung Qi and calming the Heart.

name: Licorice Root
summary: Deglycyrrhizinated licorice heals gastric and duodenal ulcers by boosting mucus and mucosal blood flow; a 1978 BMJ study found DGL as effective as cimetidine. Glycyrrhizin has antiviral activity and is used intravenously for hepatitis in Japan, and licorice gargle reduces post-intubation sore throat.
how: DGL chewable tablets 380-760 mg about 20 minutes before meals for digestive issues; this form removes glycyrrhizin and its blood pressure effect. Licorice root tea: 1-5 g dried root simmered 10-15 minutes, limited to 1-2 cups daily. In formulas, typically 3-6 g. Do not take whole licorice beyond 4-6 weeks.
safety: Major warning: glycyrrhizin causes sodium retention and potassium depletion leading to hypertension, edema and hypokalemia, with hospitalizations and deaths reported from excessive intake. Contraindicated in hypertension, heart failure, kidney disease and hypokalemia. Strongly interacts with diuretics, corticosteroids, digoxin and blood pressure medications. Avoid in pregnancy (preterm birth risk). Cap whole root at roughly 3 g (100 mg glycyrrhizin) daily; DGL avoids most of this.
origin: 'The Great Harmonizer', found in an estimated 50-70% of classical TCM formulas to moderate other herbs.

name: Dong Quai
aka: Dang Gui, female ginseng, Angelica sinensis
summary: The premier Blood tonic in TCM. Ferulic acid promotes red blood cell production and inhibits platelet aggregation, while ligustilide adds antiplatelet, antithrombotic and vasodilatory effects used in Chinese hospitals for stroke and angina. Trials of it alone failed for menopause, since TCM never uses it as a single agent.
how: Best used within a formula prescribed by a practitioner, classically Si Wu Tang with rehmannia, white peony and ligusticum. Decoction 6-12 g dried root simmered 20-30 minutes; capsules or extract 500-1000 mg two to three times daily. Traditionally simmered with chicken and goji berries as a Blood-building soup.
safety: Contains coumarins and interacts strongly with warfarin and other blood thinners. Furanocoumarins cause photosensitivity, so avoid excessive sun. Avoid in pregnancy (may stimulate uterine contractions) and during heavy menstrual bleeding, since it invigorates Blood. Mild estrogenic activity means caution in estrogen-sensitive conditions.
origin: Called 'The Female Ginseng' but used for anyone with Blood deficiency, including men.

name: Chrysanthemum
summary: Contains lutein, beta-carotene and flavonoids that protect retinal cells, with a 2015 study showing protection against UV-induced retinal damage. Chlorogenic acid gives strong free-radical scavenging, and flavonoids promote vasodilation with blood-pressure-lowering effects in animal studies.
how: Tea: steep 5-8 dried flowers in hot water 5-10 minutes, optionally with goji berries and rock sugar, one of the most popular daily teas in China. Combine with goji for a Liver and eye tonic. Eye compress: brew strong tea, soak cotton pads and rest on closed eyes 10-15 minutes.
safety: Allergic reactions occur in people allergic to ragweed, daisies or the Asteraceae family. May interact with medications metabolized by the liver. Very safe at normal tea-drinking doses, but its cooling nature does not suit those with cold digestive constitutions and frequent diarrhea.
origin: Ju Hua disperses Wind, clears Heat and 'brightens the eyes', which in TCM are the window of the Liver.

name: Cinnamon / Cassia
aka: Rou Gui, Gui Zhi, Cinnamomum cassia
summary: A 2019 meta-analysis of 18 RCTs found cinnamon significantly reduced fasting glucose, total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides while raising HDL in type 2 diabetes, at 120 mg to 6 g/day. MHCP mimics insulin, and a 2003 Diabetes Care study showed 18-29% glucose reductions.
how: Powder 1-6 g (about 1/4 to 1 tsp) daily in food, oatmeal, coffee or tea. Tea: simmer a cinnamon stick 15 minutes. Capsules 500-1000 mg cassia two to three times daily with meals for blood sugar. Add to curries, stews and baked goods.
safety: Cassia contains up to 1% coumarin, which is liver-toxic in quantity; EFSA's tolerable daily intake is 0.1 mg/kg, roughly 1-2 tsp of cassia for a 70 kg adult. Ceylon cinnamon has negligible coumarin and suits daily long-term use. May interact with diabetes medications (hypoglycemia) and with blood thinners via coumarin, and high doses can lower blood pressure. Never apply cinnamon oil neat to skin, as it burns.
origin: Rou Gui (bark) warms Kidney Yang; Gui Zhi (twigs) anchors Gui Zhi Tang, one of the most famous TCM formulas.

name: Jujube Dates
aka: Da Zao, Suan Zao Ren, Ziziphus jujuba
summary: Jujube seed (Suan Zao Ren) contains jujubosides with sedative and anxiolytic action through GABAergic and serotonergic pathways; a 2020 systematic review of 13 studies found jujube seed preparations improved sleep quality. The fruit is very high in vitamin C and gastroprotective polysaccharides.
how: Eat 3-6 dried dates daily as a snack or in teas, soups and congee. Jujube tea: simmer 5-6 sliced dates with ginger and goji berries 20 minutes. For sleep, Suan Zao Ren 15-30 g simmered, or 300-600 mg standardized extract 30 minutes before bed.
safety: Very safe in food amounts. High sugar content means diabetics should account for it, and excess may cause bloating. Suan Zao Ren may add to sedative medications. In TCM it may slow digestion in those with significant dampness or phlegm.
origin: Da Zao tonifies Spleen Qi, nourishes Blood and calms the spirit; with licorice it is a top harmonizing herb.

name: Kudzu
summary: Harvard/McLean research found puerarin cut binge drinking by 50% in a controlled lab setting, with a 2013 RCT confirming reduced beer consumption when taken before drinking. Puerarin is used intravenously in Chinese hospitals for angina and myocardial infarction.
how: For alcohol reduction, 1.5-3 g kudzu extract standardized to puerarin, taken 30-60 minutes before anticipated drinking. Root decoction: simmer 9-15 g dried root 20-30 minutes; the starchy root is also eaten. Capsules 500-1000 mg standardized extract two to three times daily.
safety: May interact with diabetes medications (hypoglycemia risk), with anticoagulants via antiplatelet effects, and with methotrexate through shared liver enzymes. It is phytoestrogenic, so use caution in estrogen-sensitive conditions such as breast cancer, endometriosis and fibroids. Otherwise well tolerated at recommended doses.
origin: Ge Gen releases the muscles of the neck and upper back and is the lead herb in the classical formula Ge Gen Tang.

name: Fo-Ti
aka: He Shou Wu, Zhi He Shou Wu, Polygonum multiflorum
summary: A famous longevity tonic containing TSG, a resveratrol-related stilbene that extends lifespan and protects neurons in animal studies and promotes melanocyte proliferation in vitro, offering a mechanism for its anti-graying reputation. A Chinese trial found processed fo-ti cut total cholesterol 20%.
how: Use only the processed form (Zhi He Shou Wu, steamed with black soybean juice); raw fo-ti is a harsh laxative and more hepatotoxic. Decoction 9-15 g processed root simmered 30+ minutes, or capsules/extract 500-1000 mg two to three times daily. Traditional use is long-term at moderate doses.
safety: Liver toxicity warning: both raw and processed fo-ti have been linked to hepatotoxicity including liver failure, with warnings issued in the UK, Australia and several European countries. Regular liver function monitoring is strongly recommended, and it should be avoided in existing liver disease and alongside hepatotoxic medications. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; may cause diarrhea, abdominal pain and nausea.
origin: A classic Jing (essence) tonic said to restore hair color and strengthen tendons and bones.

name: Sweet Wormwood / Artemisinin
summary: Tu Youyou isolated artemisinin from this herb guided by TCM texts, earning the 2015 Nobel Prize; artemisinin-based combination therapies are now the WHO first-line malaria treatment. Derivatives show iron-dependent anticancer activity in preclinical models, an early-stage complementary support area only.
how: For malaria, artemisinin-based combination therapy is prescription-only under medical supervision, never self-treatment. Traditional tea steeps fresh or dried leaves in warm (not boiling) water, which preserves artemisinin, as a supplementary approach only. Artemisinin supplements of 100-200 mg exist but quality varies enormously.
safety: Do not self-treat malaria, a life-threatening disease requiring proper care, and the WHO advises against Artemisia annua tea as monotherapy because it promotes drug resistance. Can cause nausea, vomiting, dizziness and tinnitus, and is neurotoxic at high doses (brainstem and auditory damage in animals). Embryotoxic, so absolutely avoid in pregnancy. May interact with CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 substrates.
origin: Ge Hong's 340 CE text described wringing the juice from soaked Qing Hao, a cold extraction that preserved the active compound.

name: Dan Shen
summary: Tanshinones and salvianolic acids improve circulation and are used intravenously in Chinese hospitals for acute coronary syndrome. A 2007 Cochrane review found benefit for angina when combined with conventional treatment.
how: Decoction 9-15 g; Danshen dripping pills are widely used in China. Best used under the guidance of a practitioner alongside conventional cardiac care.
safety: Strong anticoagulant interaction with warfarin: do not combine. Because it treats serious cardiac conditions, use only alongside proper medical management, never as a substitute.
origin: A classic Blood-moving herb for blood stasis and chest pain.

name: Bai Zhu
summary: Used for digestive weakness, diarrhea, edema and fatigue. Atractylone stimulates gastric motility, and the herb has been studied within formulas for IBS and chemotherapy-induced nausea.
how: Typically 6-15 g within a multi-herb decoction prescribed by a TCM practitioner rather than taken alone.
safety: No major interactions documented, but it is traditionally used in formula: consult a qualified practitioner, and inform your doctor if you take prescription medications.
origin: A core Spleen Qi tonic that dries dampness in classical Chinese formulas.

name: Huang Qin
summary: Baicalin and baicalein are potent anti-inflammatories and antivirals with strong antioxidant activity, studied in Chinese clinical trials as adjunct therapy for COVID-19 and used for inflammation, infection, anxiety and allergies.
how: Typically 6-15 g in decoction, usually as part of a formula prescribed by a TCM practitioner.
safety: Rare hepatotoxicity has been reported, so avoid in liver disease, watch for jaundice or dark urine, and use reputable products. Consult a practitioner before combining with prescription medications.
origin: A classic heat-clearing, damp-drying herb in Chinese formulas.

name: Ashwagandha
aka: Withania somnifera, Indian ginseng, winter cherry
summary: The strongest evidence is for stress: a 2012 RCT found 300 mg root extract twice daily cut serum cortisol 27.9% and anxiety scores 44%. Trials also show increased testosterone and sperm count in infertile men, greater muscle mass and strength, and a 2020 meta-analysis found improved sleep quality.
how: KSM-66 root extract 300-600 mg daily, the most studied form, or Sensoril (root plus leaf) 125-250 mg daily. Traditional method: 1 tsp powder in warm milk with honey before bed. Root powder 3-6 g daily in milk, smoothies or honey. Benefits accumulate over 4-8 weeks.
safety: Can raise thyroid hormone levels: avoid in hyperthyroidism and use cautiously with thyroid medication. May enhance sedatives, anxiolytics and immunosuppressants, and may interact with blood pressure and blood sugar medications. Avoid in pregnancy (traditionally abortifacient at high doses). Rare liver injury reported, so use caution with liver disease. Nightshade family; women with PCOS or hyperandrogenism should be cautious.
origin: A premier Rasayana and Medhya Rasayana whose name means 'smell of the horse', for the vitality it confers.

name: Tulsi / Holy Basil
aka: Ocimum tenuiflorum, O. sanctum, Queen of Herbs
summary: A 2017 systematic review of 24 studies found significant adaptogenic and anti-stress effects with cortisol modulation. A 2017 review of 9 clinical trials found reduced fasting glucose, postprandial glucose and HbA1c, and a 2014 trial found 300 mg/day improved FEV1 and PEFR in asthma.
how: Tulsi tea: steep 5-8 fresh leaves or 1 tsp dried in boiling water 5-10 minutes, 2-3 cups daily, the most traditional form. Capsules 300-600 mg standardized extract two to three times daily; tincture 30-40 drops in water two to three times daily. Chewing 5-8 fresh leaves on an empty stomach is traditional.
safety: May reduce fertility (animal studies show antifertility and anti-spermatogenic effects), so couples trying to conceive should be cautious. Eugenol slows blood clotting, so stop 2 weeks before surgery and use caution with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs. May lower blood sugar alongside diabetes medications and can enhance pentobarbital and other CNS depressants.
origin: The most sacred plant in Hinduism, a Rasayana that balances all three doshas and is grown in most households.

name: Triphala
summary: A 2017 RCT found triphala (two 525 mg tablets twice daily) improved bowel movements, consistency and straining in functional constipation better than senna with fewer side effects. A 2019 study showed increased Bifidobacterium and Lactobacillus and more butyrate; triphala mouthwash matched chlorhexidine for plaque.
how: Powder 3-6 g (1/2 to 1 tsp) in warm water before bed, the traditional method; honey softens the pungent, sour taste. Capsules or tablets 500-1000 mg two to three times daily before meals or at bedtime. Steep 1 tsp powder for a cooled mouthwash.
safety: May cause loose stools, cramping or gas at first, so start low and increase gradually. Avoid during pregnancy, since haritaki mildly stimulates the uterus. Use caution with diabetes medications, as it may lower blood sugar, and it may increase the effect of anticoagulants via amalaki's vitamin C. Not for use during acute diarrhea, which should be evaluated.
origin: Ayurveda's most prescribed formula, a Tridoshic Rasayana; Charaka Samhita links a year's use to a long life.

name: Brahmi
summary: A 2014 meta-analysis of 9 RCTs (518 subjects) found significantly improved attention, cognitive processing and working memory, with stronger effects past 12 weeks. Bacosides modulate serotonin, dopamine and acetylcholine and reduce beta-amyloid aggregation; trials also show reduced anxiety.
how: Standardized extract (KeenMind, Synapsa, Bacopin) 300-450 mg daily at 50% bacosides, taken with a fat-containing meal since bacosides are fat-soluble. Traditional Brahmi ghrita cooks the powder in ghee, 1 tsp daily. Powder 5-10 g in warm milk or water. Allow 8-12 weeks for full benefit.
safety: Commonly causes GI upset, nausea, cramping and bloating, so take with food. May raise thyroid hormone levels, so use caution in hyperthyroidism, and may cause drowsiness and enhance CNS depressants. Possible interaction with cholinergic drugs such as donepezil and rivastigmine and with anticholinergics. It increases gastric acid, so use caution with active ulcers, and avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding.
origin: A leading Medhya Rasayana named after Brahma, traditionally given to students to sharpen memory and learning.

name: Neem
summary: Azadirachtin, nimbin and nimbidin are active against bacteria including MRSA, fungi, viruses and parasites. A 2011 RCT found neem mouthwash reduced plaque and gingivitis as effectively as chlorhexidine, and reviews find leaf extract lowers blood glucose in animal and small human trials.
how: Neem leaf capsules 300-600 mg two to three times daily for internal use. Leaf tea: steep 5-10 dried leaves 10 minutes (extremely bitter). Apply diluted neem oil externally for fungal infections, eczema, acne or as insect repellent. Chew a fresh neem twig (datun) as a natural toothbrush; crushed leaf paste treats skin conditions.
safety: Never ingest neem oil, which is toxic internally and has poisoned children; only leaves and bark are used internally, and it is not recommended orally for infants and young children. Can lower blood sugar sharply alongside diabetes medications. Reduces fertility in both sexes and may cause miscarriage, so avoid when trying to conceive, in pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Immunostimulatory, so avoid with immunosuppressants or autoimmune disease; high or prolonged doses can damage liver and kidneys.
origin: Called 'Sarva Roga Nivarini' (curer of all ailments); every part of the tree is used, and twigs were toothbrushes.

name: Moringa
summary: A 2019 systematic review of 10 clinical trials found leaf powder at 1-8 g/day significantly reduced fasting glucose in type 2 diabetes, and a 2000 study found 8 g daily for 40 days lowered total cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides. Moringin is a potent NF-kB inhibitor, and reviews support galactagogue use.
how: Leaf powder 1-2 tsp (3-6 g) daily in smoothies, soups or sprinkled on food, starting at 1/2 tsp. Capsules 400-800 mg two to three times daily. Cook fresh leaves like spinach; steep 1 tsp dried leaves 5 minutes as tea; drumstick pods feature in South Indian cooking.
safety: Avoid moringa root, root bark and seed extracts, which contain toxic, paralytic spirochin. May lower blood sugar and blood pressure, so monitor with relevant medications, and may interact with thyroid medications (goitrogens) and CYP3A4-metabolized drugs. High doses have shown antifertility effects in animals. Start small, since some people get digestive upset.
origin: In Ayurveda Shigru reduces swelling, destroys worms and kindles digestive fire; every part of the tree is used.

name: Amla
summary: One of the richest natural vitamin C sources, uniquely stabilized by tannins. A 2012 RCT found 500 mg extract twice daily comparable to atorvastatin 20 mg for lowering cholesterol, LDL and triglycerides while raising HDL, and studies show reduced fasting glucose and HbA1c.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily in warm water with honey, the traditional dose. Fresh juice 20-30 mL on an empty stomach each morning. Chyawanprash 1-2 tsp daily; capsules 500-1000 mg extract two to three times daily. Warm amla oil massaged into the scalp and left 30-60 minutes for hair.
safety: Very high vitamin C may cause GI upset or diarrhea at high doses, and its acidity can aggravate reflux. May lower blood sugar alongside diabetes medications and may enhance anticoagulants through antiplatelet activity. High vitamin C increases iron absorption, so use caution in hemochromatosis. One of the safest Ayurvedic herbs at food-level doses.
origin: Charaka Samhita calls it the best rejuvenative; it is the base of Chyawanprash and one of the three Triphala fruits.

name: Shatavari
summary: A 2018 systematic review found shatavari raised prolactin and milk production in animal and small human studies, and a 2018 RCT found 250 mg root extract twice daily significantly reduced hot flashes and night sweats. Animal work shows gastroprotection comparable to ranitidine.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily in warm milk with ghee and honey, the traditional preparation that aids absorption. Capsules 500-1000 mg two to three times daily; tincture 2-4 mL two to three times daily. Shatavari ghrita (cooked in ghee) is the classical reproductive-health preparation.
safety: Avoid if allergic to asparagus. It may be estrogenic, so avoid in estrogen-receptor-positive breast cancer and other estrogen-sensitive conditions. It may have diuretic properties and could interact with diuretics. Avoid in acute kidney inflammation, and it is not suited to acute diarrhea or heavy mucus conditions. May cause weight gain from its heavy, nourishing quality.
origin: Ayurveda's premier female reproductive tonic, the counterpart to ashwagandha, nourishing reproductive tissue and Ojas.

name: Guggul
summary: Guggulsterones antagonize the farnesoid X receptor governing cholesterol metabolism; Indian trials showed 10-27% reductions in cholesterol and triglycerides, but a rigorous 2003 JAMA RCT found guggul raised LDL in a Western population. A 2003 pilot study matched tetracycline for nodulocystic acne.
how: Standardized extract 500-1000 mg three times daily at 2.5-5% guggulsterones. Classical formulas include Kaishore Guggulu for joint inflammation and gout, Triphala Guggulu for detoxification, and Yogaraj Guggulu for Vata-type pain, taken as an Ayurvedic practitioner directs.
safety: The 2003 JAMA finding of LDL elevation means lipid monitoring is recommended. It stimulates thyroid function, so avoid in hyperthyroidism, and it interacts with thyroid medications, blood thinners (antiplatelet effect) and cardiovascular drugs, reducing the efficacy of propranolol and diltiazem. May interact with oral contraceptives via estrogen metabolism. Avoid in pregnancy and breastfeeding; can cause nausea, vomiting, loose stools, hiccups and rash.
origin: A key Lekhana (scraping) resin; the Sushruta Samhita described its use for atherosclerosis over 2,500 years ago.

name: Arjuna
summary: A landmark 2001 RCT found bark powder 500 mg every 8 hours improved ejection fraction, exercise tolerance and NYHA class in chronic stable heart failure, and a 2002 crossover study matched isosorbide mononitrate for angina. Arjunolic acid cuts myocardial oxidative stress and inhibits ACE.
how: Traditional Arjuna Kshira Paka: boil 3-6 g bark powder in one cup milk and one cup water until reduced to one cup, drunk on an empty stomach each morning. Bark powder 3-6 g daily in warm water or milk; capsules 500 mg extract two to three times daily; Arjunarishta 15-30 mL after meals.
safety: Never use as a substitute for emergency cardiac care; heart conditions need proper medical management and this is best used under supervision. May lower blood pressure, so monitor with antihypertensives, and it may interact with cardiac glycosides such as digoxin, anticoagulants and blood pressure medications. Can cause constipation, headache or body aches; pregnancy safety is not established.
origin: The primary Ayurvedic heart tonic (Hrdya), named after the Mahabharata warrior and described in the Charaka Samhita.

name: Turmeric (Ayurvedic use)
summary: Ayurveda's Haridra is used for inflammation, skin disease, diabetes and anemia. The traditional Golden Paste combining turmeric with black pepper and ghee or coconut oil was validated millennia later by bioavailability research showing piperine and fat dramatically increase curcumin absorption.
how: Golden Paste: turmeric powder with black pepper and coconut oil or ghee. Haldi doodh: turmeric in warm milk with black pepper, ghee and honey before bed for inflammation, respiratory infections and sleep. Turmeric-and-water or oil paste is applied to cuts, burns and skin conditions; Nasya drops turmeric in warm ghee into the nostrils for sinus congestion.
safety: Same cautions as concentrated curcumin: it inhibits platelet aggregation, so use caution with anticoagulants, and it may lower blood sugar. Avoid concentrated supplements with gallstones or bile duct obstruction. High doses raise oxalate (kidney stone risk) and may interact with certain chemotherapy drugs, so consult your oncologist. Food and paste amounts are safe for nearly everyone.
origin: Classified as bitter, pungent and heating, balancing all three doshas and used for Kushtha (skin disease) and Prameha.

name: Cardamom
summary: A 2009 RCT found 3 g cardamom powder daily for 12 weeks significantly reduced systolic and diastolic blood pressure, raised antioxidant status 90% and increased fibrinolytic activity in stage 1 hypertension. 1,8-cineole is anti-inflammatory, and the spice is a validated carminative.
how: Chew a pod after meals for digestion and fresh breath. In chai, crush 2-3 pods with ginger and cinnamon. Powder 1/4-1/2 tsp in coffee, oatmeal or baking; for blood pressure, 3 g (about 1 tsp) powder daily per the clinical study. Cardamom milk with saffron is a traditional nighttime drink.
safety: Very safe at culinary doses. May interact with anticoagulant medications. Gallstone patients should use caution, since it stimulates bile flow. High doses can cause GI discomfort, and allergic reactions are rare but possible.
origin: 'The Queen of Spices', Tridoshic in Ayurveda and used to kindle digestive fire and treat vomiting and asthma.

name: Black Pepper / Piperine
summary: Piperine inhibits CYP3A4, CYP2D6, CYP1A2 and P-glycoprotein, raising curcumin absorption by 2,000% plus meaningful boosts to CoQ10, B6, beta-carotene and selenium. It is also thermogenic, anti-inflammatory via NF-kB and COX-2, and increases brain serotonin and dopamine in animal studies.
how: Use freshly ground pepper liberally in cooking, where piperine content is highest. Trikatu: equal parts black pepper, long pepper and dried ginger, 1/4-1/2 tsp with honey before meals. BioPerine supplements 5-20 mg taken with other supplements; always pair with turmeric. A pinch in honey soothes sore throat and congestion.
safety: Critical drug interaction: piperine raises absorption of medications too, dramatically increasing blood levels of phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline, rifampin, some chemotherapy drugs, immunosuppressants such as cyclosporine and statins. Tell your doctor if you supplement with piperine. It increases gastric acid, so avoid high supplemental doses with ulcers or GERD. Cooking amounts are safe for virtually everyone.
origin: 'The King of Spices', a Trikatu ingredient that kindles Agni, destroys Ama and reduces Kapha.

name: Ghee
summary: Contains 3-4% butyric acid, the short-chain fatty acid that fuels colonocytes, reduces intestinal inflammation and supports gut barrier integrity, plus CLA (up to 5x more in grass-fed). It enhances absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and phytonutrients like curcumin, validating cooking herbs in ghee.
how: Use 1-2 tsp as a cooking fat; its 485 F smoke point suits high heat. Mix herbal powders such as turmeric, ashwagandha or brahmi into warm ghee to boost absorption. A traditional morning ritual takes 1 tsp warm ghee on an empty stomach. Make it by heating unsalted butter until the milk solids brown, then straining. Keep to 1-3 tsp daily.
safety: High in calories and saturated fat, so portion control matters and those with high cholesterol, heart disease or obesity should use it sparingly and monitor lipids. Trace dairy proteins remain, so highly dairy-allergic people should test cautiously. Ayurveda considers equal proportions of ghee and honey incompatible, and Kapha-dominant constitutions should limit intake.
origin: Charaka called ghee the best of all oils; it is the primary Anupana (carrier) for Ayurvedic medicines and Panchakarma.

name: Coconut Oil
aka: Narikela Taila, Cocos nucifera, virgin coconut oil
summary: About 50% lauric acid, converted to antimicrobial monolaurin active against S. aureus, Candida, H. pylori and enveloped viruses. A 2016 systematic review found oil pulling reduced S. mutans, plaque and gingival inflammation comparably to chlorhexidine, and a 2014 RCT improved skin hydration in dry skin.
how: Oil pulling: swish 1 tbsp virgin oil for 15-20 minutes each morning before brushing, then spit into the trash. Cook with 1-2 tsp at medium heat (smoke point 350-400 F). Apply directly to skin or hair as a moisturizer or mask. Blend 1 tsp into coffee for MCT energy; choose virgin oil.
safety: Roughly 82% saturated fat, the highest of any common dietary fat. A 2020 Circulation meta-analysis found it significantly raises LDL versus non-tropical plant oils, and the AHA advises against it as a primary cooking fat for cardiovascular patients, so those with heart disease or high LDL should use it sparingly. Comedogenic on the face for some, calorie-dense at 120 cal/tbsp, and rare allergy is possible.
origin: Narikela pacifies Vata and Pitta and is the base oil for Abhyanga massage and Kerala's traditional healing.

name: Guduchi / Giloy
summary: A potent immunomodulator used for immune deficiency, fever, diabetes, gout and allergies. It contains berberine and tinosporin with anti-inflammatory and antiviral effects, and a 2020 study during COVID-19 found giloy extract improved immune markers.
how: Extract 500-1000 mg daily, or 15-30 mL fresh juice daily.
safety: Indian case reports from 2021-2022 raised concerns about liver injury, with contamination by other plants suspected, so buy only from reputable, verified sources and avoid with existing liver disease. As an immunostimulant, use caution with immunosuppressants and autoimmune conditions.
origin: Called 'Amrita', the nectar of immortality, in Ayurveda.

name: Pippali / Long Pepper
summary: Used for respiratory conditions, digestion and enhancing the bioavailability of other remedies. It contains piperine like black pepper plus piperlongumine, which has anticancer properties studied in preclinical models only.
how: Powder 1-3 g daily, classically as one third of the Trikatu formula with black pepper and dried ginger.
safety: Same critical drug interaction concerns as black pepper and piperine: it raises blood levels of many medications including phenytoin, propranolol, theophylline, rifampin, cyclosporine, statins and some chemotherapy drugs. Inform your doctor before supplementing.
origin: One of the 'three pungents' in Trikatu, Ayurveda's classic digestive and metabolic formula.

name: Shankhpushpi
summary: Another Medhya Rasayana used for anxiety, insomnia, cognitive decline and epilepsy. Animal studies show anxiolytic, memory-enhancing and anticonvulsant effects via GABAergic and cholinergic mechanisms, with limited but promising human data.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily, or 500 mg standardized extract daily.
safety: May interact with anti-epileptic and thyroid medications, so consult your prescriber before use. Given the sedative profile, use caution with other CNS depressants.
origin: A classical Ayurvedic brain rejuvenator for calming the mind.

name: Manjistha
summary: Used in Ayurveda for skin conditions, blood purification and lymphatic congestion. Alizarin and purpurin have anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and hepatoprotective effects, and it is used clinically for acne, eczema and pigmentation disorders, though modern trial data are limited.
how: Powder 3-6 g daily, or 500-1000 mg extract daily.
safety: Use caution with anticoagulants. It harmlessly stains urine and sweat red or brown, which can be mistaken for bleeding.
origin: A classical Ayurvedic Raktashodhaka (blood-cleansing) herb for the skin and lymph.
